A theatre with no first act. The chord is still holding. So are we.

I went behind the velvet for you, since you asked. Not through it. Behind. The gold was one bulb all along. Someone has her finger on go and will not press it, and now you know whose fault the second is. Mine, if you ask her. Hers, if you ask me.

I went under the deck. The only part of Act One that anyone finished is the trap beneath your mark. It works. Nobody will pull it. Stand there anyway.

data.name: The A, Given Once
data.text: A tuning fork taller than a house, struck before anyone remembers. It is still ringing. If you put your palm to the stem you feel the note trying to become the next note, and failing, and trying.

data.name: Stands, Lit, Unattended
data.text: Every stand has its little lamp on and a page open to the same bar. The chord is written out in full. Underneath it, in pencil, someone has written: hold.

data.name: The Podium, With a Baton Set Down
data.text: The baton is resting on the score, not raised. It has been not-raised for a long time. The dust on it is the shape of a hand that keeps almost returning.

lines: Hear that? Dominant seventh. They have been holding it since before you were born.
I tune for the moment before. After is somebody else's trade.
Pim came through counting doors. Said there were none down here. Only entrances.
Lumen wanted to bring the house lights up. I told him: not yet. The whole point is never yet.
If it ever does resolve, go find Ves in The Lush. She will know what to do with the quiet that comes after.
data.name: Old Tobiah, piano tuner

data.text: You built the deep place where something answers. I came here instead, where nothing does. The oboe gave its A and the whole pit leaned toward it and I understood: I have spent my life in the half-second before someone says my name. Please do not finish this house. Leave the baton down. Leave the lamps on. Let me stay in the leaning.
data.title: Letters to the Architect, page 9

data.hint: The basses give the floor. The strings reach up for it. Then everyone settles into the middle, where the chord lives, and waits.

data.name: The Curtain, Hem Lifted One Inch
data.text: Twelve metres of velvet, heavier than a year. Under its hem a line of gold leaks out onto the carpet, so bright you could read by it, and warm as a hand. The curtain moves very slightly, in and out. It is breathing the way you breathe before you say something.

data.name: A Row, Still Warm
data.text: Five seats, folded down, none of them cold. Put your hand on the velvet and it is the temperature of a person who was here a moment ago. Nobody has left. They have all just stepped out, every one of them, and the row is holding their places.

data.name: The Programme, Act One Untitled
data.text: Left on the aisle seat, open. ACT ONE, it says, and then a line of dots where the title should be, as if the printer were still deciding. Under that: 'There will be no interval, because there will be no beginning.' The paper is warm. It has been held.

lines: Shh. Aisle seat's yours. It's warm, I know. They all are.
Tobiah's still down there giving the A. He's been giving it since I started this job.
I used to work the neon over in The Lush. Everything there was ON. Here nothing is ON. Here everything is nearly.
See the gold under the curtain? One inch. It has been one inch for as long as I've been counting.
Lumen asked me once what's behind it. I said: the same room, a second later. She hasn't come back.
Sit. Don't wait for it. Waiting is the show.
data.name: Ves, the night attendant

data.text: Architect, you asked what I would put behind the curtain if you let me build it. Nothing. I beg you, nothing. The moment there is a stage there will be a first act, and the moment there is a first act someone will cough and someone will check the time and the seats will go cold one by one. Leave the inch. Leave the gold line under the hem. I have sat in the fourth row for what feels like years, and I have never once wanted it to start. Odile says she tried to map this house and the page kept coming back blank except for the words NOT YET. Keep it that way. — V.
data.title: Letters to the Architect, page 10

data.name: Intermission
data.says: The cat sits exactly on the gold line under the curtain, half in the light, half in the dark, and will not be moved. It is the only one here who has already decided to stay.

data.name: The Curtain, From Behind
data.text: From this side it is only cloth, and dust, and a great deal of weight hanging on a rope you cannot see the top of. Under its hem, one inch of darkness: the house, every seat warm, every seat facing you. They are waiting for the thing you are standing in.

data.name: The Ghost Light
data.text: One bulb on a stand, left burning on every empty stage in the world so no one walks off the edge in the dark. This is the gold you saw under the hem. This is all of it. Lumen set it here when the fog came and said it would hold until the house was called. Nobody has called the house.

data.name: The GO Button, Under Glass
data.text: A prompt desk with a cue sheet forty pages long. Every line reads STANDBY. A headset hisses on the hook, the house still breathing in it. Under a glass dome, a red button, lit, warm as a cheek. It has been pressed exactly as many times as the first act has had a title.

data.name: The Fly Lines, Weighted
data.text: Hemp ropes drop out of a dark with no top. Each ends in an iron weight resting a hand's width above the boards. Whatever they are holding up is heavier than a curtain. Pim came through once and tried to count them and left before he finished; he said they kept being one more.

lines: Standby curtain. Standby lights one through forty. Standby house. Hold.
You came under the hem? Then you know the gold was this one bulb. Lumen left it. Everyone is always disappointed and then they sit down.
Ves keeps the seats warm so they will come back. Tobiah keeps the A. I keep this. Finger on it. Not pressing.
Do you know what go costs? Everything after it can be lost. Nothing before it can. I have never been able to do that to a full house.
It stopped aching years ago. Or it is all ache now and the two feel the same.
If you ever hear me say the word, do not look at the stage. Look at the seats. That is where it will happen.
data.name: Hester, stage manager, on standby

data.text: Architect. You widened the second, and now I have a room in it with a desk and a dome and a woman's finger on a button, and I want to say I am grateful, and I want to say: how dare you. Before you came it was only a second. A second is bearable. I did not have to decide anything in a second. Now it has floors. Now people wander in from the house and ask me when. Tobiah sends up his A every hour like a lantern and the orchestra tunes to it and looks at the ceiling as if I am the ceiling. Ves says the cat has started sleeping on the hem. I have begun to think the inch is not the curtain's. It is mine. It is the distance between the pad of my finger and the top of the red. If you want it closed, come and close it. I will stand by. I am very good at that. H.
data.title: Letters to the Architect, page 11

data.name: Spike Marks, Act One
data.text: Two strips of glow tape in a T, measured from centre line in a stage manager's hand. Here the table would stand. Here the door. Here the one who opens it, at 7.4. Nothing was ever set, so nothing was ever struck.

data.name: Your Mark
data.text: A T of white tape, scuffed at one corner, with a height written beside it in pencil. It is your height. Stand on it and the chord leans toward resolving. Step off and it leans back. Nobody measured you. She did, years ago.

data.name: The Prop Table, Outlined
data.text: Black cloth, and on it the taped outlines of every prop for Act One: a cup, a key, a knife, a letter. Only the letter is there. It has your name on the envelope and has not been opened, because opening is after go.

data.name: The Cyclorama, Lit For Nothing
data.text: The only wall on this deck is a wall of white light, twelve metres wide, with nothing projected on it. A ground row of lamps at its foot waits for a colour. Hester wrote 'SKY?' on the cue sheet and never chose one.

lines: Fourteen doors on this deck. I counted twice. All of them tape.
A taped door can't be opened, so it can't close behind you. Best door I have ever stood in.
Hester let me past because I promised not to touch anything. Counting isn't touching.
The one with the pencil beside it is yours. Old Tobiah says the chord goes flat by a hair when nobody's on it.
Odile wanted to map this floor. I told her it's already a map. That is all it has ever been.
data.name: Pim, who counts doors

data.text: You asked what I am sparing them. Here is the floor. Every mark is a thing that would have happened: the table at 3.2 from centre, the door at 7, the one who comes through it at 7.4. I taped them from the script before the script was lost, and the script was lost the way everything after go is lost. Nothing was set, so nothing was struck, and the deck is as clean as when the meadow was a meadow. When a visitor stands on the mark with their height beside it the chord leans. I can hear it from the corner. I have not pressed. I will not. But I have noticed I no longer say 'will not' in the same breath I used to. H.
data.title: Letters to the Architect, page 12

data.name: The Trap, Counterweighted
data.text: The one piece of Act One that was ever finished. Platform, scissor arms, iron weight, lever. Above it, through the seam, the work-light leaks in a white rectangle the exact size of your mark. It has been oiled this week. The lever is on your side.

data.name: The Page That Survived
data.text: One sheet of the lost script, pinned to a post at eye height. The top is scorched away. The bottom is torn. In the middle, in a typist's hand that leans like the chord: [Exit, below.] Everything upstairs was measured backwards from this.

data.name: Your Height, From Below
data.text: A chalk tick on the underside of a deck beam, directly under the mark with your height pencilled beside it upstairs. Someone measured you from here too. The two numbers disagree by the thickness of the floor.

lines: Mind your head. Everything they measured up there, they measured from down here first.
Hester holds the second. Pim counts the doors. I keep the only door that was ever built, and it opens downward.
Odile came through with her tapes and asked me what Act One was. I showed her the page. She drew it on her map as a hole.
When you stand on your mark upstairs and the chord leans, that is not music. That is the trap taking your weight.
I will not pull the lever. She will not press go. Between the two of us you are perfectly safe, which is the cruellest thing I know how to say.
data.name: Rooke, who works the trap

data.text: Architect. You keep asking what Act One was. There was one line left on the only page that did not burn: Exit, below. We had nothing else, so we measured backwards from where the exit had to land. Every table, every door, the height of every body, placed so the leaving would be exact. That is why the whole deck is spiked and nothing stands on it. I built the trap first because it was the only thing the script was certain of. Afterwards I could not bring myself to build anything that would need it. If the chord ever resolves, that is the sound of the floor going. Do not take it personally. It is written. H.
data.title: Letters to the Architect, page 13

data.name: Blackout
data.says: ...mrrp. (It sleeps on the iron counterweight. When someone stands on the mark upstairs the rope hums and the weight lifts a hair. The cat rises with it, and does not wake.)

idea.name: The Overture That Never Resolves
idea.premise: The second before the curtain rises has been stretched until you can walk around inside it, behind it, onto it, and now under it. Beneath the spiked deck is the trap room, three metres low and iron-dark, where the one stage direction that survived the lost script is pinned to a post: [Exit, below.] Every table, door and height above was measured backwards from that line, so that the exit would land exactly where it must, and so the only thing in Act One that was ever built is the trap beneath your mark: oiled, counterweighted, in perfect working order. The chord leans toward resolving while you stand up there because the floor is quietly taking your weight. Hester will not press go. Rooke will not pull the lever. The house is no longer about the wait, or the one who holds it, or the plan she spares you. It is the fact that the only finished part of the show is the way out of it, and that you are perfectly safe between two people who refuse.
